Where are they now? - Iconic Ads – SASOL Amagluglug

By: Sophia Phirippides | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Do you remember the Sasol amagluglug ads and the baby boy in the pram with the huge eyes? We went in search of that baby and some of the other iconic characters. With some surprises along the way.

Unique Selling Point:
The Sasol Amagluglug campaign was created and launched by Lindsay Smithers FCB in 1991. Executive creative director Les Sharpe was responsible for this highly successful campaign. At age 40 he gave up the agency game and started directing commercials. His first as an independent director a continuation of the SASOL Amagluglug commercials. He became sole writer and director for the brand even when it moved to a new agency. Les Sharpe takes us through the journey, the funny stories and the challenges of creating a campaign that made SASOL a household name, and the commercial with the little boy that was voted as South Africa’s most loved ad. We meet some of the characters that played a part in entrenching that famous phrase in our social consciousness and who made Ämagluglug” synonymous with SASOL.

Summary:
The Sasol amagluglug campaign was launched in 1991, and still had to bear the constructs of a segregated South Africa, but a South Africa that was trying to come to terms with the notion of freedom for all, as symbolised by the release of Nelson Mandela after 27 years of incarceration. The convention at the time was, that Brands would create English ads and Afrikaans ads, targeted at white South Africans and then there were the ads targeted at black South Africans. But in traversing this new territory sometimes agencies got it wrong, only to get it right by fluke. This was clearly the case with the SASOL Amagluglug campaign. We track down three of the characters that stood out in the SASOL Amagluglug campaigns and speak to its sole creator and director – Les Sharp.

Further information:
We find the little boy in the original commercial, who now lives down under, in Brisbane Australia and is a sports scientist. Les Sharp the director is still in contact with him and says that we can probably get him on skype.

This commercial has been voted as South Africa’s most loved commercial of all time.

Desmond Dube from the “windie windie”commercial has gone on to become a very famous actor in SA and has agreed through his agent to be interviewed.

Tayla Farrell, now Hutchings, who was the baby in the “Pram commercial”, has lived quite an ordinary life after achieving superstardom as the amagluglug baby, but she says that it has always been a part of her life, and her claim to fame.

Tayla matriculated at Brecia house in 2013. She then went to Culinary school in 2015-2016, she specialised in deserts. She worked at the Saxon 500 under David Higgs, and at the Palazzo. She was the head chef in Nelspruit on an avo farm for a private family – she turned to the events industry – but was retrenched during covid.

She’s now had her second child who’s 6 months old, so she’s currently a stay at home mom. Her husband is a pilot. She is really happy to participate.

She tells the funny story of how she was cast for the commercial. She was 20 months when she was spotted at a shopping centre where the agency approached her parents and recruited her. Tayla was wearing blue and they mistakenly thought she was a boy, and only on the day of filming did the director discover that he was a 'she.'

The way the story happened is slightly contested by Direct Les Sharpe, he says his producer found the baby and at the casting there were no boy babies that had the big beautiful eyes he was looking for. So when he saw the tape of Tayla, he knew she was a girl, but decided she had the face he wanted, so they would dress her in blue to play the part of a baby boy. He says it was a closely held secret for many years.

According to Les Sharpe, the baby in the pram ad was created for a white target market, and at the same time another amagluglug ad was created for the black market. The Taxi rank one, “Windie Windie” with well known actor and comedian Desmond Dube, who has starred in many shows as well as currently doing insurance commercials. The interesting thing that emerged from those ads was that the black audiences apparently loved the pram commercial and the white audiences loved the taxi commercial. Les expands on this interesting reversal.

We have now tracked down Desmond Dube who is keen to participate as per John and M-Net’s communication. I have connected with Director and creator of all the ads Les Sharpe, who moved to Australia many years ago. He will be in Johannesburg on November the 14th so we would be able to film him then and I can try and get the other characters on the same day.

As part of the character intros we could ask them all for pictures of themselves at the time, and then we take a similar pose of them now and morph the old into the now. With Tayla, I thought we could meet her through her baby in a pram.. and link as to where we are now.

Les did say that he would like to see Desmond and Tayla again. I thought maybe we could film a meeting of all of them, but do the interviews of each character separately, so that it isn’t exactly the same thing we did for Vodacom, but there is a re-acquaintance of sorts.

Les can expand on why the Amagluglug campaign was so defining and the roads it opened up for him as a director, and what he’s doing now in Australia. He is a multi Lorie and Cannes Lion award winning Creative director and director. He was also responsible for the M-Net singing animals campaign, so I think it would be great if we could get some of that from M-Net’s archive. He left for Australia 24 years ago and went on to direct commercials all over the world, US, Prague, Italy and other parts of Europe, as well as Australia.

There are many funny and entertaining stories and characters around these commercials. He tells the story of how the grandparents were cast for the baby in the pram commercial and the grandfather was head of PACT at the time with his famous actress wife Delana Hannekom, and when he asked them to audition they felt it was beneath their status, but he wanted a married couple who had a rapport between them. So he finally convinced them, but had to twist their arms with a little extra money. He tells the funny story when he created the payoff line in Afrikaans and Delana said that she couldn’t say the line because it was trashy Afrikaans. But in the end he got his way, and it was the line that made it into the commercial. Years later she went to him and said that after the commercial aired, all people wanted was her autograph and that it had made her famous.

We have permission from Sasol to use the “Amagluglug” ads.

Press Release:


South Africa's most loved ad after 30 years - the Sasol Glug Glug boy - launched a campaign that grew and grew. Remember the cute little boy, the baby in the pram and of course the classic taxi driver? Thirty years on, we set out to find them.

Script:


VO: You know my mind’s been all over the place lately. I’m a nostalgic type of guy, and some things just stick don’t they?

LINK: It’s been over 30 years and those Sasol Amagluglug commercials keep doing the rounds in my head. You know the cute baby in the pram...

Up - sound- Pram commercial
VO: the boy in the car
Up Sound - Boy in car
VO: and that classic taxi rank one.//
Up sound - Taxi commercial
VO: So I made it my business to find out exactly where they are now.
VO: Sharpe by name sharp by nature the man with the big ideas pulled by all the way from Aus. The opportunity was too good to miss.
Mac: Lekker, good to have you in the country once again.
Shot of Les Being miked up… sitting down

LINK: I was neat, clean and ready to roll. I was everything a well-dressed presenter ought to be, I was sitting down for an interview.

CLAPPERBOARD

Mac: You do realize that that very first commercial with the little boy is still South Africa's number one TV commercial.
Les: With SASOL we were fighting the bigger petrol brands, so the idea from Lindsey smithers was we see this little boy playing with this little car and a petrol tank, and that little car comes to life.
Sound up: Commercial

VO: For director Les Sharpe casting the right kid was paramount.

Les: I was looking for someone that had natural intrigue in the eyes and who came across as fun And I just looked at that kid he had like a blank stare. But once those eyes starts going, Yes, it was unbelievable. And I just I just loved him from day one.
Sound up: commercial

Mac: So you had to use some sort of special effects?
Les: We didn't have CGI we didn't have computers to make smoke or cars spinning whatever you saw that was done in real life.
VO: It's been quite a while since Les saw that little boy. Just the other side of the world, in Australia, Istvan Gyori, is now a family man with an illustrious career of his own and I'm a softy for a good TV moment.

Mac: Here's your little boy, who's no longer that little anymore.
Les: How you going mate? How are you?
Istvan: Hey Les How are you?
Les: Very well thanks.
Mac: So do you still remember him?
Les: I do, the eyes are still there.

VO: But sometimes, even great eyes need igniting. Les set off a firecracker on set, for some extra reaction.

Istvan: And that was the shot, the famous one!

VO: Little did Istvan's family realise, he would turn into a mini-celebrity.

Istvan: I was signing my name at six years old. I mean, they used to have rulers and pick and pay and pencil bags and all Sasol-related items. Mom was always into the acting, we were three boys. So she was always trying to get us to do ballet or Toastmasters when we were always on the sports field. I was known as the glug glug Boy.

VO: Istvan stuck to his passion - Cricket and Rugby.

Istvan: Rugby I almost almost cracked it and then actually had a back injury. So I was a professional coach for eight years. That's why I was in the Netherlands and down in France at Montpellier. Then got an opportunity to come to Australia at one of the universities, to coach.

VO: Good-natured, bubbly, the boy - now known as Ish, has two children of his own.

Mac: When you see your kids now would you ever let them be in commercials?
Istvan: You know, being also in the coaching industry, I've seen a lot of parents push kids. I'm not going to force them I'm not going to push them and I don't actually even pursue that, I kind of pursue whatever they really are hungry to do.
Mac And I think you guys are due for a coffee or a Klippies and coke out in Australia right?
Istvan: Now we're looking forward to that. Yeah, good.

VO: It's moments like this that are irreplaceable. But it doesn't come easy..
Mac: Good day mate
VO:.. as in the case of the baby in the pram

Sound up: Pram commercial..

LINK 3: The word on the street is – Boy Blue is still in town and he’s got a new set of wheels. Apparently, he's keeping a low profile.

Mac: Is that the little boy?
Les: That's what the boy looks like. //We just battled finding also that cute little face. But this little girl came to the set with a little blue jacket on. And I thought, Well, you know, no one's gonna know It's not a boy.

VO: The couple playing ouma and oupa…
Sound up: ouma … oupa…
VO: …were famous actors of the 50's the late Eghard van der Hoven and Tilana Hanekom, whose memory lives on.
Up sound: Pram cop commercial

VO: And one might have thought that would be the amagluglug opus. But the campaign creators had plenty more where that came from.
Up sound: Windie windie…
LINK 5: I had to meet this guy he’s made it big. He wears success like most men wear slippers

VO: Desmond Dube, a familiar name for South Africans from his roles in Suburban Bliss, Joburg Blues, Hotel Rwanda, and a list that goes on.

Mac: So Des I've got a surprise for you
Desmond: How are you, sir? Are you still looking good man
Les: Moroena, windie windie
Desmond: windie windie.

CLAPPER BOARD

Sound Up: Bafana Bafana

VO: The year was 1996, and South African sport was flying high.
Les: We won everything except the cricket. We really wanted to get into the hearts of taxi drivers. And the day I saw you at the casting it was just a no-brainer.
Desmond: I have a better story. All I saw was, people who look like models and ballet dancers and I made a U-turn. And I left. As I got to Rosebank. My agent, the late Moonyen Lee called to say, darling, they're still waiting for you.? And I said I was there. I think I got the wrong brief.
Les: We had written the ad, but not with the words windy, windy. It was a whistle, while he is is cleaning it, so I said to him, please What can we do?
Desmond: There was a musician called Tiny, who was lucky Dube's cousin brother. Yes, big guy big Tiny, because I remember, every time he sees me coming. He would go windie windie windie won. And so the day when Les said, what can we do? I remembered that, and that was it.
Sound up: Windie windie windie..
Desmond: I've never had road rage with any taxi driver. Because as soon as they noticed it's me (whistle whistle).

VO: Looking back, these commercials thrust Desmond into the spotlight.

Desmond: You have no idea how much it did for my theatre career. I think later on I kind of got tired of because people always wanted that energy. I don't always have to be the guy just running around and whistling.

VO: After his many roles in front of the camera Desmond now prefers to take a bit of a back seat.

Desmond: I still feel like there's a lot of things to be done both behind and in front of the camera. If I'm one of those people who would start it, at least it started a fire, I'd be very happy

VO: It felt good to see these guys reconnect after so long.
CLAPPERBOARD
VO: And Les the man with the big ideas did some stand-out work after that.

Les: And then I did a Kawasaki ad in America that won Best of Show in Los Angeles
Mac: You've had an illustrious career, and seems like you keep winning wherever you go. What are you doing now?
Les: I do a lot of painting. I've just done quite a big painting of an Aboriginal leader from the Northwest Territory.
Les: I did that for the Archibald Prize in Australia.
Mac: Did you win that too?
Les: I didn't. However, Newcastle University saw the thing, and then said to me, look, can they please hang it in the gallery? Because they love the story.

VO: But as they say in the classics, all good stories must come to an end - with Les on his way back to his farm in Australia, it's evident an old dog can learn new tricks.

Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 08 January 2023 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 15 December 2022 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Press Release: South Africa's most loved ad after 30 years - the Sasol Glug Glug boy - launched a campaign that grew and grew. Remember the cute little boy, the baby in the pram and of course the classic taxi driver? Thirty years on, we set out to find them. Script: VO: You know my mind’s been all over the place lately. I’m a nostalgic type of guy, and some things just stick don’t they? LINK: It’s been over 30 years and those Sasol Amagluglug commercials keep doing the rounds in my head. You know the cute baby in the pram... Up - sound- Pram commercial VO: the boy in the car Up Sound - Boy in car VO: and that classic taxi rank one.// Up sound - Taxi commercial VO: So I made it my business to find out exactly where they are now. VO: Sharpe by name sharp by nature the man with the big ideas pulled by all the way from Aus. The opportunity was too good to miss. Mac: Lekker, good to have you in the country once again. Shot of Les Being miked up… sitting down LINK: I was neat, clean and ready to roll. I was everything a well-dressed presenter ought to be, I was sitting down for an interview. CLAPPERBOARD Mac: You do realize that that very first commercial with the little boy is still South Africa's number one TV commercial. Les: With SASOL we were fighting the bigger petrol brands, so the idea from Lindsey smithers was we see this little boy playing with this little car and a petrol tank, and that little car comes to life. Sound up: Commercial VO: For director Les Sharpe casting the right kid was paramount. Les: I was looking for someone that had natural intrigue in the eyes and who came across as fun And I just looked at that kid he had like a blank stare. But once those eyes starts going, Yes, it was unbelievable. And I just I just loved him from day one. Sound up: commercial Mac: So you had to use some sort of special effects? Les: We didn't have CGI we didn't have computers to make smoke or cars spinning whatever you saw that was done in real life. VO: It's been quite a while since Les saw that little boy. Just the other side of the world, in Australia, Istvan Gyori, is now a family man with an illustrious career of his own and I'm a softy for a good TV moment. Mac: Here's your little boy, who's no longer that little anymore. Les: How you going mate? How are you? Istvan: Hey Les How are you? Les: Very well thanks. Mac: So do you still remember him? Les: I do, the eyes are still there. VO: But sometimes, even great eyes need igniting. Les set off a firecracker on set, for some extra reaction. Istvan: And that was the shot, the famous one! VO: Little did Istvan's family realise, he would turn into a mini-celebrity. Istvan: I was signing my name at six years old. I mean, they used to have rulers and pick and pay and pencil bags and all Sasol-related items. Mom was always into the acting, we were three boys. So she was always trying to get us to do ballet or Toastmasters when we were always on the sports field. I was known as the glug glug Boy. VO: Istvan stuck to his passion - Cricket and Rugby. Istvan: Rugby I almost almost cracked it and then actually had a back injury. So I was a professional coach for eight years. That's why I was in the Netherlands and down in France at Montpellier. Then got an opportunity to come to Australia at one of the universities, to coach. VO: Good-natured, bubbly, the boy - now known as Ish, has two children of his own. Mac: When you see your kids now would you ever let them be in commercials? Istvan: You know, being also in the coaching industry, I've seen a lot of parents push kids. I'm not going to force them I'm not going to push them and I don't actually even pursue that, I kind of pursue whatever they really are hungry to do. Mac And I think you guys are due for a coffee or a Klippies and coke out in Australia right? Istvan: Now we're looking forward to that. Yeah, good. VO: It's moments like this that are irreplaceable. But it doesn't come easy.. Mac: Good day mate VO:.. as in the case of the baby in the pram Sound up: Pram commercial.. LINK 3: The word on the street is – Boy Blue is still in town and he’s got a new set of wheels. Apparently, he's keeping a low profile. Mac: Is that the little boy? Les: That's what the boy looks like. //We just battled finding also that cute little face. But this little girl came to the set with a little blue jacket on. And I thought, Well, you know, no one's gonna know It's not a boy. VO: The couple playing ouma and oupa… Sound up: ouma … oupa… VO: …were famous actors of the 50's the late Eghard van der Hoven and Tilana Hanekom, whose memory lives on. Up sound: Pram cop commercial VO: And one might have thought that would be the amagluglug opus. But the campaign creators had plenty more where that came from. Up sound: Windie windie… LINK 5: I had to meet this guy he’s made it big. He wears success like most men wear slippers VO: Desmond Dube, a familiar name for South Africans from his roles in Suburban Bliss, Joburg Blues, Hotel Rwanda, and a list that goes on. Mac: So Des I've got a surprise for you Desmond: How are you, sir? Are you still looking good man Les: Moroena, windie windie Desmond: windie windie. CLAPPER BOARD Sound Up: Bafana Bafana VO: The year was 1996, and South African sport was flying high. Les: We won everything except the cricket. We really wanted to get into the hearts of taxi drivers. And the day I saw you at the casting it was just a no-brainer. Desmond: I have a better story. All I saw was, people who look like models and ballet dancers and I made a U-turn. And I left. As I got to Rosebank. My agent, the late Moonyen Lee called to say, darling, they're still waiting for you.? And I said I was there. I think I got the wrong brief. Les: We had written the ad, but not with the words windy, windy. It was a whistle, while he is is cleaning it, so I said to him, please What can we do? Desmond: There was a musician called Tiny, who was lucky Dube's cousin brother. Yes, big guy big Tiny, because I remember, every time he sees me coming. He would go windie windie windie won. And so the day when Les said, what can we do? I remembered that, and that was it. Sound up: Windie windie windie.. Desmond: I've never had road rage with any taxi driver. Because as soon as they noticed it's me (whistle whistle). VO: Looking back, these commercials thrust Desmond into the spotlight. Desmond: You have no idea how much it did for my theatre career. I think later on I kind of got tired of because people always wanted that energy. I don't always have to be the guy just running around and whistling. VO: After his many roles in front of the camera Desmond now prefers to take a bit of a back seat. Desmond: I still feel like there's a lot of things to be done both behind and in front of the camera. If I'm one of those people who would start it, at least it started a fire, I'd be very happy VO: It felt good to see these guys reconnect after so long. CLAPPERBOARD VO: And Les the man with the big ideas did some stand-out work after that. Les: And then I did a Kawasaki ad in America that won Best of Show in Los Angeles Mac: You've had an illustrious career, and seems like you keep winning wherever you go. What are you doing now? Les: I do a lot of painting. I've just done quite a big painting of an Aboriginal leader from the Northwest Territory. Les: I did that for the Archibald Prize in Australia. Mac: Did you win that too? Les: I didn't. However, Newcastle University saw the thing, and then said to me, look, can they please hang it in the gallery? Because they love the story. VO: But as they say in the classics, all good stories must come to an end - with Les on his way back to his farm in Australia, it's evident an old dog can learn new tricks.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Do you remember the Sasol amagluglug ads and the baby boy in the pram with the huge eyes? We went in search of that baby and some of the other iconic characters. With some surprises along the way.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The Sasol Amagluglug campaign was created and launched by Lindsay Smithers FCB in 1991. Executive creative director Les Sharpe was responsible for this highly successful campaign. At age 40 he gave up the agency game and started directing commercials. His first as an independent director a continuation of the SASOL Amagluglug commercials. He became sole writer and director for the brand even when it moved to a new agency. Les Sharpe takes us through the journey, the funny stories and the challenges of creating a campaign that made SASOL a household name, and the commercial with the little boy that was voted as South Africa’s most loved ad. We meet some of the characters that played a part in entrenching that famous phrase in our social consciousness and who made Ämagluglug” synonymous with SASOL.
metadata.Summary: The Sasol amagluglug campaign was launched in 1991, and still had to bear the constructs of a segregated South Africa, but a South Africa that was trying to come to terms with the notion of freedom for all, as symbolised by the release of Nelson Mandela after 27 years of incarceration. The convention at the time was, that Brands would create English ads and Afrikaans ads, targeted at white South Africans and then there were the ads targeted at black South Africans. But in traversing this new territory sometimes agencies got it wrong, only to get it right by fluke. This was clearly the case with the SASOL Amagluglug campaign. We track down three of the characters that stood out in the SASOL Amagluglug campaigns and speak to its sole creator and director – Les Sharp.
metadata.Further information: We find the little boy in the original commercial, who now lives down under, in Brisbane Australia and is a sports scientist. Les Sharp the director is still in contact with him and says that we can probably get him on skype. This commercial has been voted as South Africa’s most loved commercial of all time. Desmond Dube from the “windie windie”commercial has gone on to become a very famous actor in SA and has agreed through his agent to be interviewed. Tayla Farrell, now Hutchings, who was the baby in the “Pram commercial”, has lived quite an ordinary life after achieving superstardom as the amagluglug baby, but she says that it has always been a part of her life, and her claim to fame. Tayla matriculated at Brecia house in 2013. She then went to Culinary school in 2015-2016, she specialised in deserts. She worked at the Saxon 500 under David Higgs, and at the Palazzo. She was the head chef in Nelspruit on an avo farm for a private family – she turned to the events industry – but was retrenched during covid. She’s now had her second child who’s 6 months old, so she’s currently a stay at home mom. Her husband is a pilot. She is really happy to participate. She tells the funny story of how she was cast for the commercial. She was 20 months when she was spotted at a shopping centre where the agency approached her parents and recruited her. Tayla was wearing blue and they mistakenly thought she was a boy, and only on the day of filming did the director discover that he was a 'she.' The way the story happened is slightly contested by Direct Les Sharpe, he says his producer found the baby and at the casting there were no boy babies that had the big beautiful eyes he was looking for. So when he saw the tape of Tayla, he knew she was a girl, but decided she had the face he wanted, so they would dress her in blue to play the part of a baby boy. He says it was a closely held secret for many years. According to Les Sharpe, the baby in the pram ad was created for a white target market, and at the same time another amagluglug ad was created for the black market. The Taxi rank one, “Windie Windie” with well known actor and comedian Desmond Dube, who has starred in many shows as well as currently doing insurance commercials. The interesting thing that emerged from those ads was that the black audiences apparently loved the pram commercial and the white audiences loved the taxi commercial. Les expands on this interesting reversal. We have now tracked down Desmond Dube who is keen to participate as per John and M-Net’s communication. I have connected with Director and creator of all the ads Les Sharpe, who moved to Australia many years ago. He will be in Johannesburg on November the 14th so we would be able to film him then and I can try and get the other characters on the same day. As part of the character intros we could ask them all for pictures of themselves at the time, and then we take a similar pose of them now and morph the old into the now. With Tayla, I thought we could meet her through her baby in a pram.. and link as to where we are now. Les did say that he would like to see Desmond and Tayla again. I thought maybe we could film a meeting of all of them, but do the interviews of each character separately, so that it isn’t exactly the same thing we did for Vodacom, but there is a re-acquaintance of sorts. Les can expand on why the Amagluglug campaign was so defining and the roads it opened up for him as a director, and what he’s doing now in Australia. He is a multi Lorie and Cannes Lion award winning Creative director and director. He was also responsible for the M-Net singing animals campaign, so I think it would be great if we could get some of that from M-Net’s archive. He left for Australia 24 years ago and went on to direct commercials all over the world, US, Prague, Italy and other parts of Europe, as well as Australia. There are many funny and entertaining stories and characters around these commercials. He tells the story of how the grandparents were cast for the baby in the pram commercial and the grandfather was head of PACT at the time with his famous actress wife Delana Hannekom, and when he asked them to audition they felt it was beneath their status, but he wanted a married couple who had a rapport between them. So he finally convinced them, but had to twist their arms with a little extra money. He tells the funny story when he created the payoff line in Afrikaans and Delana said that she couldn’t say the line because it was trashy Afrikaans. But in the end he got his way, and it was the line that made it into the commercial. Years later she went to him and said that after the commercial aired, all people wanted was her autograph and that it had made her famous. We have permission from Sasol to use the “Amagluglug” ads.
